newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Oil imports seen hurting Asian refining margins.
newsitem.headline: Oil imports seen hurting Asian refining margins.

text.p: Oil product imports threaten to eat into the margins of Asian refiners who have been enjoying stronger returns than their U.S. and European counterparts, analysts say.
"In this kind of commodity market, it's difficult to enjoy high profitability for long periods," said Seoul-based analyst Bill Hunsaker of ING-Barings.

The average return for refining Dubai crude oil in Singapore rose to 78 U.S. cents per barrel in February, up $1.47 from January when refiners were running at a loss, the Paris-based International Energy Agency (IEA) said earlier this month.
Complex reprocessing margins rose to $3.43 per barrel, an increase of $1.72, the IEA said.
Complex margins in northwest Europe for Brent crude were at a low 71 cents while in the U.S. Gulf, returns for West Texas Intermediate crude were at 76 cents, the IEA said.
Using the IEA model for estimating margins, Singapore's returns have risen to $1.33 per barrel for basic refining and $4.66 for complex refining.
Singapore's returns were built on an appreciable fall in crude prices while product prices remained little changed.
But industry sources in Singapore said the relatively strong product prices were turning into a liability as refiners in the West looked to Asia to sell surplus production.
Prices for almost all petroleum products including diesel, fuel oil and naphtha, were poised to fall, resulting in weaker margins, they said.
A Kuala Lumpur-based analyst with a foreign broking house was cautious over the prospects for refining margins over the next few months.
"The recovery may not be sustainable as some factors may be temporary. Normally after the winter months you see a price dip, but it will pick up if there is insufficient inventory," the analyst said.
Strong profit margins so far this year in Singapore -- Asia's main swing refinery centre -- were built partly on low regional stocks that buoyed product prices.
Those stocks have now been replenished, so Asia might not be able to absorb imports from Europe and the Middle East without prices falling.
Diesel prices could be hardest hit with up to one million tonnes of imports expected to hit Asian shores during April and May.
The imports were also encouraged by refinery closing for maintenance work.
"When they (refineries) recommence operations, the flow will come back, and that is why we see the recovery not sustaining," the Kuala Lumpur-based analyst said.
Hunsaker said refiners should see margins peaking in March. April and May should be steady at relatively high levels because refiners would still be processing cheaper crude.
"Oil input costs should decline, but the rate of decline of product prices is slower," Hunsaker said.
He said the profit potential for Asian refineries would be kept in check by record South Korean exports as the full impact of a massive refinery buildup there hits the market this year.
"For two to three years it will have excess capacity, but then will be absorbed by the domestic market," Hunsaker said.
